author: Miriam Webber
title: Australian Defence Force looks to anonymous reporting of sexual violence, amid new complaints - NewsBreak
text:
By Miriam Webber ,
1 days ago
CANBERRA — Australia’s Defence Force will review its anonymous reporting options for sexual harassment and sexual assault, as part of a broad strategy enforcing better treatment of serving women and veterans, released days after the Department of Defence was accused of failing to “clean up” its culture.
Released on the evening of Oct. 15 — more than a month after veteran groups told POLITICO its publication had been delayed — the Women Veterans Strategy responds to a need to include and advance more women as a matter of operational necessity, as Australia looks to rapidly scale up defense capability.
The strategy commits Defence to inquiring “into the effectiveness of anonymous reporting options including awareness, uptake and impact compared to alternative approaches.”
It comes just days after a video recording device was found on the Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin, reportedly in a women's bathroom , prompting independent Sen. Jacqui Lambie to call for an independent disciplinary body to investigate military sexual violence in place of military police.
“This is a culture that unfortunately Defence has not been able to clean up and it hasn’t even come close,” Lambie told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.
“It has been a substantial problem for a very, very long time … the only way we’re going to be able to stop this is by taking it out of Defence’s hands and having an independent body that actually deals with this.”
Women Veterans Australia Chair Llani Kennealy said she was pleased to see the strategy released, but called for the federal government to commit to “dedicated resources, clear accountability and independent oversight to ensure its commitments translate into meaningful outcomes for women veterans.”
The HMAS Leeuwin incident also follows the filing of a class action on behalf of women who served in the force over more than 20 years, seeking compensation for sexual harassment, harassment on the grounds of sex, discrimination in employment and victimisation.
Women now make up 21% of Australia’s permanent forces, but officials want to attract more recruits as the country tries to meet a goal of 69,000 permanent personnel, up from around 61,000 today .
“The participation, inclusion and advancement of women are therefore not only matters of equity and representation, but operational necessities that directly contribute to Defence capability, preparedness and warfighting effectiveness,” the strategy reads.
The ADF will also be forced to make its gender pay gap public in a bid to improve pay for serving women.
While the civilian part of Defence is already required to report gender pay gap data to the Workplace Gender Equality Agency annually, the ADF is not subject to this requirement. Data from the 2021 to 2022 financial year put the gap at 11.8% for permanent force salaries and 45.7% for retirement funds.
The Department of Veterans’ Affairs will meanwhile establish the role of a principal women’s adviser, and commission research on the long-term reproductive health impact of military service, after pleas from Lambie and other women veterans to address gaps in funded care for injuries acquired during service.
summary: CANBERRA — Australia’s Defence Force will review its anonymous reporting options for sexual harassment and sexual assault, as part of a broad strategy enforcing better treatment of serving women and veterans, released days after the Department of Defence was accused of failing to “clean up” its culture. The strategy commits Defence to inquiring “into the effectiveness of anonymous reporting options including awareness, uptake and impact compared to alternative approaches.”
